items.bodyEn: Numazu, the twelfth post town, sits where the Kano River meets Suruga Bay: a fishing port as well as a lodging town, and from the late 1770s the castle town of the Mizuno lords. Hiroshige's print shows pilgrims beside the river at dusk under a full moon, one carrying a huge long-nosed tengu mask for the Kompira shrine.
items.sourceNote: Hiroshige, Numazu: Twilight (1833–34); Dai Nihon Chimei Jisho (1900–07)

items.bodyEn: The tsu of Numazu, written 津, is an old word for a landing place or harbor; numa is a marsh, so the name means marsh-harbor. The same tsu opens tsunami, literally harbor wave, because the wave does its damage where the boats are tied up. Many place names ending in tsu along the Japanese coast were once ports.
items.sourceNote: Kōjien, entries 津 and 津波

items.bodyEn: The kanji of omou, to think, is 思. Its top looks like a rice field, but in the oldest forms it was 囟, the soft spot on a baby's skull, standing for the head. Beneath it sits 心, the heart. Head over heart: for early scribes, thinking happened in both. Picture the field as a brain and it sticks.
items.sourceNote: Shuowen Jiezi, entry 思 (囟 over 心); Kangxi Dictionary

items.titleEn: The day you decide is lucky
items.bodyEn: Omoitatta ga kichijitsu: the day you make up your mind is the auspicious day. In other words, start now rather than wait for a better moment. Notice the grammar of this station: omoitatta is a plain past form standing before ga, as if it were a noun, the day I decided. Sayings often drop the noun.
items.ja: {思|おも}い{立|た}ったが{吉日|きちじつ}
items.kana: おもいたったがきちじつ
